name: Pine resin (pitch)
habitat: Anywhere pines grow. Look for hardened amber beads on trunk wounds and old branch scars.
identify: True pines carry needles in BUNDLES held by a papery sheath at the base — 2, 3 or 5 to a bundle depending on species.
Resin is sticky, amber to white, and smells strongly of turpentine.

lookalikes.name: Yew
lookalikes.danger: Lethal. Every part except the red aril flesh is highly toxic; there is no antidote and death can be sudden. Yew needle 'tea' has killed people.
lookalikes.tell: Yew needles are SINGLE, flat and soft with a pointed tip, attached individually in two flat rows — never in bundles with a sheath. Yew bears a soft red berry-like aril, not a woody cone, and the bark is flaky red-brown.

lookalikes.name: Norfolk Island pine, Australian 'pines', podocarps
lookalikes.danger: Not a pine; do not assume pine properties or edibility.
lookalikes.tell: No bundled needles with a basal sheath.

preparations.method: Warm a bead of hardened resin between the fingers until it softens, and dab it directly onto a small clean wound.
preparations.for_use: Sealing and disinfecting a small cut or crack; it also seals a blister that has torn.

preparations.method: Melt resin gently with about twice its volume of animal fat or oil; strain out bark through cloth; add a little beeswax to firm it. Never boil it over open flame.
preparations.for_use: A keeping antiseptic dressing for cuts, cracked skin and small burns.

preparations.method: Steep chopped GREEN needles in hot (not boiling) water for 10 minutes.
preparations.for_use: Vitamin C; a warming drink. Identify the tree first — this is the preparation the yew confusion kills people with.

preparations.method: Resin-soaked wood (fatwood) shaves into tinder that lights wet.

cautions: Identify the tree before making ANY needle preparation. Yew is the fatal error and it grows in the same landscapes.
Pregnant women should avoid pine needle preparations; some species are associated with abortion in livestock.
Resin on a deep or dirty wound seals contamination in. Clean and irrigate first — see `wound-clean-and-dress`.
Take resin from existing wounds on the tree; cutting a tree to bleed it wounds it for your convenience.
evidence: Resin's antibacterial activity is well documented, and a standardized spruce-resin salve has been trialled clinically for wound healing. The needle-tea vitamin C content is real but modest.
